name: Helicoprion
fact: A bizarre shark with a buzz-saw tooth whorl in its lower jaw! It looked like an underwater chainsaw. Scientists thought the fossil was fake for decades. Absolutely alien-looking and totally real.
know: For a century nobody knew where its spiral of teeth went — on the snout, the tail, the back fin? CT scans in 2013 found jaw cartilage around a whorl: it sat inside the lower jaw like a circular saw. It was a relative of ratfish, not a true shark.

name: Dimetrodon
fact: NOT a dinosaur — went extinct 40 million years BEFORE dinosaurs! More related to YOU than dinosaurs.
know: Not a dinosaur. It has one opening in the skull behind each eye, the mark of the synapsids — the branch that leads to mammals. Dimetrodon is more closely related to you than to T. rex, and it died out 40 million years before the first dinosaur.
discovery: Cope (1878) named species Dimetrodon incisivus, rectiformis, gigas.
keyResearchers: Cope, E.D. (1877–1878), Kemp, T.S. (1982), Botha-Brink & Smith (2011)
citation: Cope, E.D. (1878). Descriptions of new extinct vertebrata. Proceedings APS 17:147–167.

name: Gorgonopsid
fact: Top predators with saber teeth — 50 million years before saber-toothed cats! Probably warm-blooded with fur-like covering. If you trace your family tree back 260 million years, you get to creatures like these.

name: Scutosaurus
fact: A heavily armored plant-eater that looked like a giant turtle mixed with a rhino. It lived in the hot, dry interior of Pangaea. When the Great Dying came, its whole family was wiped out forever.

name: Moschops
fact: A big plant-eating synapsid with a super thick skull for head-butting. Part of the therapsid lineage heading toward mammals. It probably had some fur. Our very, very distant grandparent.

name: Mesosaurus
fact: One of the first synapsids to return to water! It had flippers and a long tail for swimming. Proof that land animals were trying water travel before the Permian ended. Part of the mammal family tree.
know: A small freshwater reptile found only in southern Africa and eastern South America. Alfred Wegener used it in 1915 as evidence that the two continents had once been joined: it could not have crossed an ocean.

name: Glossopteris
fact: A seed-fern tree that covered Gondwana! When it died by millions during the Great Dying, its wood turned to coal. This plant dominated half the Permian world, then vanished almost entirely in the extinction.
know: When the bodies of Captain Scott's party were found in Antarctica in 1912, beside them lay 16 kg of rock they had refused to abandon. It contained Glossopteris leaves — proof that Antarctica was once warm, forested and joined to other continents.

name: Lystrosaurus
fact: Nicknamed the survivor, Lystrosaurus is the only large land animal known to have dominated Earth after a mass extinction. After the Great Dying wiped out 96% of all species, Lystrosaurus made up nearly 95% of all land vertebrate individuals on the planet for millions of years.
know: The same pig-sized animal is found in South Africa, India and Antarctica — lands now separated by thousands of kilometres of ocean it could not have swum. After the Great Dying it made up as much as nine-tenths of all land vertebrates in some places.

name: Edaphosaurus
fact: A large sail-backed plant-eater that lived before the dinosaurs. The cross-bar spines on its sail distinguish it from its predatory sail-backed cousin Dimetrodon. The sail may have regulated body temperature by acting as a solar panel on cold mornings.

name: Estemmenosuchus
fact: A huge therapsid with multiple horns sprouting from its skull like a nightmare reindeer. Despite its fearsome look Estemmenosuchus ate plants. As one of the largest land animals of its time it represents the therapsid radiation that eventually produced mammals.

name: Prionosuchus
habitat: Rivers and swamps of South America
fact: Possibly the largest amphibian ever to live - longer than a large crocodile. A temnospondyl with a long snout full of sharp teeth, Prionosuchus hunted fish and smaller vertebrates in Permian rivers of what is now Brazil.

name: Coelurosauravus
fact: The first known gliding vertebrate - a small reptile with elongated ribs supporting a wing membrane like a modern flying dragon lizard. Coelurosauravus soared between trees in the Permian forest canopy, 80 million years before pterosaurs took to the air.

name: Cotylorhynchus
fact: A huge barrel-shaped plant-eater with a tiny head — its body was one enormous gut for digesting tough plants.

name: Inostrancevia
fact: The largest gorgonopsian, with sabre teeth 12 cm long. Fossils found in South Africa in 2023 suggest it moved south as the world fell apart in the run-up to the Great Dying.

name: Diictodon
fact: A small, tusked burrower that dug corkscrew-shaped tunnels. Pairs have been found curled up together at the bottom of their burrows.

name: Suminia
fact: The oldest known tree-climbing vertebrate, with grasping hands and a gripping tail.

name: Seymouria
fact: A sturdy animal that blurs the line between amphibians and reptiles: built for dry land, but its young still had amphibian-style ear features.

name: Diplocaulus
fact: An amphibian with a boomerang-shaped head. The wide head may have worked like a wing in the water — or simply made it too big to swallow.

name: Meganeuropsis
fact: The largest insect that ever lived — a griffinfly, cousin of dragonflies, with wings as wide as an eagle's are long.

name: Euchambersia
fact: A small hunter with a deep pit in its face and grooved canine teeth.
debate: The pit and grooves look like a venom system, as in some snakes. A 2017 scan of the skull supported this; others think the grooves are simply ridges.

name: Ophiacodon
fact: One of the largest animals of the early Permian, with a long, deep skull — an early member of the mammal line.

name: Heleosaurus
fact: An adult and four young found curled together — the oldest known evidence that a land animal looked after its young.

name: Eunotosaurus
fact: A turtle ancestor with no shell yet — just very broad ribs.
know: A 2016 study of its arms and ribs found it was a burrower. The broad ribs gave a stable base for digging. The turtle shell seems to have started as a digging tool, not armour.

name: Bunostegos
fact: A cow-sized plant-eater with bony knobs on its head, and one of the first reptiles to stand with its legs straight under its body.

name: Anteosaurus
fact: The biggest land predator of its time, with a huge, thick-boned skull. It was once thought to lurk in water like a crocodile; leg studies show it could run.

name: Tapinocephalus
fact: A huge plant-eater with a skull roof up to 10 cm thick — almost certainly for head-butting contests.

name: Orobates
fact: A plant-eater known from a skeleton and its own matching footprints — so well that in 2019 scientists built a walking robot of it, “OroBOT”, to find out how it moved.

name: Platyhystrix
fact: An amphibian with a tall sail on its back, like a small Dimetrodon — a sail that evolved separately.

name: Xenacanthus
fact: A freshwater shark with an eel-like body and a long spine sticking backwards from its head.

name: Hovasaurus
fact: A water reptile with a tall, flat tail for swimming. Pebbles in its stomach worked as ballast to help it dive.

name: Moschorhinus
fact: A big-headed hunter that survived the Great Dying — but after it, it was smaller and died out within a million years. Survival was not the same as recovery.

name: Varanops
fact: A slim, fast hunter shaped like a monitor lizard, with curved teeth for slicing.
debate: Varanopids have long been counted as early mammal relatives. A 2020 study argued they were really early reptiles; the question is open.

name: Casea
fact: A small-headed, barrel-bodied plant-eater. The big belly held the long gut needed to break down tough leaves — a new way of life for land animals.

name: Sphenacodon
fact: A close cousin of Dimetrodon with a low ridge along its back instead of a tall sail. Same killer teeth, no sail — a clue that the sail was not needed for hunting.

name: Secodontosaurus
fact: A sail-back with a long, narrow snout like a fox’s — perhaps for snatching fish, or pulling small animals out of burrows.

name: Tetraceratops
fact: Known from one small skull with bony bumps on its face. It may be the oldest known therapsid — the group that leads to mammals.
debate: Whether it is a true therapsid or a late sail-back relative has been argued since the 1990s. There is only the one skull.

name: Raranimus
size: Known from part of a snout
fact: A piece of snout from China with two pairs of canine teeth. It is the most primitive therapsid known, and it hints that therapsids began in the northern lands.

name: Biarmosuchus
fact: An early therapsid hunter, long-legged and lightly built, with big canine teeth. Its legs were held more upright than a sail-back’s — a step towards the way mammals walk.

name: Titanophoneus
fact: Its name means “titanic murderer”. A heavy-skulled hunter with long front teeth for gripping and big canines for killing.

name: Eodicynodon
fact: The earliest dicynodont: a small plant-eater that already had the group’s trademark — a turtle-like beak and two tusks.

name: Dicynodon
fact: “Two dog teeth”: a beak, two tusks and no other teeth. Dicynodonts were the most common plant-eaters on Earth at the end of the Permian.

name: Gorgonops
fact: The animal the gorgonopsians are named after — “Gorgon face”. Sabre teeth, a jaw that opened extremely wide, and long legs for running down prey.

name: Lycaenops
fact: “Wolf face”: a wolf-sized sabre-tooth with long, slim legs held closer under the body than a reptile’s.

name: Rubidgea
fact: The biggest African gorgonopsian, with huge sabre teeth and a skull as long as a lion’s whole head and neck. The top predator of its world — wiped out in the Great Dying.

name: Procynosuchus
fact: One of the first cynodonts, the “dog teeth” — the branch that leads to mammals. It already had the start of a bony roof to its mouth, which lets an animal breathe while it chews.
debate: Its flexible back and paddle-like tail bones made some scientists think it swam like an otter; others doubt it.

name: Sinophoneus
fact: A big-headed hunter from western China, a cousin of Anteosaurus in Africa and Titanophoneus in Russia — the same kinds of animals across Pangaea.

name: Endothiodon
fact: A beaked plant-eater found in South Africa, India and Brazil. One animal on three continents is evidence that they were joined — as the map shows.
